newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts debates trade ban against Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts debates trade ban against Indonesia.

text.p: A Nobel Peace Prize winner urged a Massachusetts legislative committee on Thursday to adopt a measure that would effectively ban companies that do business in Indonesia from doing business with the commonwealth.

"Smaller states than Massachusetts, such as Norway, have contributed to the peace process ... So this state by itself, its prestige, its technology has an enormous affect outside its borders," 1996 Nobel Peace Prize winner Jose Ramos-Horta told reporters after testifying before the committee.

Ramos-Horta, a former East Timorese journalist who fled his homeland shortly after Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony in 1975, urged the committee to pass the measure which also includes ordering the state's $18 billion pension fund to divest itself of all Indonesian assets.

Massachusetts public pension funds hold about $11 million either directly or indirectly in Indonesian assets. It is unclear if the bill, which has 80 co-sponsors in the state legislature, would also force the funds to shed assets in financial institutions that do business with Indonesia.

The archipelago nation has a $6 billion trade relationship with the United States. Massachusetts ranks 16th in the United States in total exports to Indonesia, shipping nearly $50 million in products during 1996, according to bill's author, Representative Antonio Cabral.
Companies such as Raytheon, Gillette and Reebok International Ltd, all headquartered in Massachusetts, do business with both the Commonwealth and Indonesia.

Raytheon's spokesman, Robert McWade, said the company was talking to the Indonesia government about three projects -- modernising their airports, environmental controls and electricity generation -- "that will improve the lives of Indonesians and create jobs for people in Massachusetts."
Ramos-Horta, who has said earlier he opposed economic sanctions, said the situation has evolved, so "the regime leaves no alternatives for moderates such as myself."

"If corporations in the United States want to affect the situation, affect the life of the poor, they should give direct assistance to the NGOs (non-governmental organisations) that are really working with the poor people," he said.
Legislative sources said opposition to the measure was building. Members of the legislature have received a letter from the European-American Chamber of Commerce opposing the bill.

But the legislators are also aware that Portugese are the state's fourth largest ethnic group. Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 days after Portugal granted it independence. In 1976 Indonesia annexed the island as its 27th province, but the United Nation's never recognised the move.
